blocks.text: Metals are hard, rigid substances that are good conductors of heat and electricity. They are malleable and ductile, so they can be rolled into sheets or drawn into wires without breaking. Steel is used in bridges and buildings because of its strength, aluminium in aircraft bodies because it is light, and copper in electric wires because it conducts electricity very well.

Metals are found in the earth's crust. Less reactive metals such as gold and platinum occur in the free (metallic) state. More reactive metals such as sodium, aluminium, iron and copper occur in the combined state as ores; for example haematite, Fe2O3, is an ore of iron. Ores are not pure compounds but mixtures of the desired metal compound with impurities and earthy materials called gangue.

blocks.title: Metallurgy
blocks.text: Metallurgy is the science of extracting metals from their ores and making them pure for better use. The reactivity and nature of the metal decide the extraction method.

items: Mining: the metal ore is dug out of the earth (Figure 31.2 shows iron ore mining and a lump of haematite).
Ore concentration: the ore is freed from impurities as far as possible.
Conversion of the concentrated ore to the metal oxide, by roasting or calcination.
Reduction of the metal oxide to the metal.

blocks.text: Roasting is heating a sulphide ore in an excess supply of air: 2ZnS(s) + 3O2(g) -> 2ZnO(s) + 2SO2(g). Calcination is heating a metal carbonate ore in little or no air to convert it into the oxide: ZnCO3(s) -> ZnO(s) + CO2(g).

Reduction of the metal oxide is the most important step. For less reactive metals (below carbon in the reactivity series), carbon is used as the reducing agent. Carbon is first converted into carbon monoxide, which then removes the oxygen from the metal oxide to leave the free metal. For iron ore: C + 1/2 O2 -> CO, then Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2.

This method cannot be used for metals more reactive than carbon, because carbon cannot reduce their oxides. For such metals (for example Na, K and Al) an electrolytic method is used: the metal compound is melted and an electric current is passed through it, which needs a lot of energy. The positive metal ions move to the negative electrode (cathode), where they gain electrons and form the metal. Electrolysis is also used to obtain very high purity in less reactive metals such as copper.

blocks.alt: A flow chart of six boxes joined by arrows: mining, ore concentration, conversion to oxide (with the roasting and calcination equations for zinc ores), reduction to metal (carbon monoxide reducing Fe2O3; electrolysis for Na, K, Al), refining (copper 99.99% pure for wiring) and alloying.

blocks.long_description: Follow the arrows from the ore in the ground to a pure metal or alloy. The method used for reduction depends on whether the metal is above or below carbon in the reactivity series.

blocks.text: Refining: the metal obtained after reduction is usually of high purity, but some uses need very pure metal; for example, copper for electrical wiring must be 99.99% pure. A metal can be refined by thermal, chemical or electrochemical methods. Alloying is mixing two or more metals, or a metal with a non-metal, to give a homogeneous mixture. This changes the microstructure of the metal and improves properties such as strength, corrosion resistance, and electrical or magnetic behaviour.
